In 2013, on my first trip abroad, a Huawei billboard at Munich Airport thrilled me.

In 2020, the United States took on Huawei as a nation.


When I first went abroad, seeing Europeans use Chinese phones and other electronics felt a bit magical. Now Xiaomi, Huawei and Lenovo are everywhere.


Does this show that China is undergoing a revival?

Yes and no.


I believe most people can clearly feel that China’s international standing has risen. As it gradually gains a say in world affairs, it can no longer quietly get rich while keeping its head down. One false step and it becomes everyone’s target. China has always been a special case in the jungle of nations, a minority of one, so it inevitably has a vulnerable constitution. A true revival isn’t just about GDP growth, or every country using things made in China. The world also has to recognize your culture and values, as it did in the thousand-odd years from the height of the Tang dynasty to the reign of the Qianlong Emperor. The might of a whole nation can make technology and wealth take off, but the softer things have to seep in slowly. More importantly, we need to build our own culture and values, and that is hard to do while wealth is piling up so fast. The pandemic is a window: it’s a good thing that people around the world can see more clearly what is happening in China. But exporting culture, values or even ideology during this period would be rushing it, and could very well backfire.

So the revival is happening, but completing it is a long road.

I hope that day comes soon.
